title: Accumulated area: adding up thin strips
explanation:
At constant speed, distance = speed × time: the area of a rectangle under a flat speed graph. When speed changes, slice time into thin strips. On each strip the speed is nearly constant, so each strip contributes a thin rectangle of area (speed) × (short time). Add them up and you approximate the distance; thinner strips give better approximations. 3Blue1Brown puts the punchline simply: area under the curve is equal to the distance traveled [1].

The same picture works for any rate. Area under a litres-per-second graph is litres. The units of the area are (height units) × (width units).

One twist: when the graph dips below the axis, the integral counts that part as negative. OpenStax: area is always positive, but a definite integral can still produce a negative number, a *net signed area* [2]. So $\int_a^b r(t)\,dt$ measures **net** accumulation: what flowed in minus what flowed out.
keyIdeas: Accumulated amount = area under the rate graph.
Approximate with thin rectangles; thinner strips give better estimates.
Area units = height units × width units (m/s × s = m).
Parts below the axis count as negative: integrals give net change.

workedExample.problem: A cyclist's speed is $v(t)=2t+1$ m/s for $0\le t\le4$ s. How far does she travel?
steps: Sketch: a straight line rising from $v(0)=1$ to $v(4)=9$, all above the axis.
Rough estimate with four 1-second strips using left heights: $1+3+5+7=16$ m. The speed keeps rising, so this underestimates.
The exact region is a trapezoid: $\frac{1+9}{2}\times4=20$.

pitfalls: Forgetting units: the area's units are height units times width units.
Counting area below the axis as positive when the question asks for net change.
Treating a coarse rectangle estimate as exact.
